Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Maria grew up in a small apartment in East Los Angeles, the space her mother turned into a fortress after the nights the boy who had promised to protect her began to strike. She remembers the sharp sting of a knotted bruise on her forearm and the way the fluorescent lights flickered like a warning signal. Those fragments of terror do not fade; when the memory surfaces she finds herself reaching instinctively for the cleaning supplies that had once symbolized safety, wiping surfaces with a rhythm that feels like a defensive chant. The compulsive act of scrubbing, she believes, steadies the chaos that memory tries to throw into her present. In this way, the recollection of abuse fuels her drive to keep everything in order, and the order, in turn, becomes a refuge from the haunting images. The memory of those nights is not confined to the past; it awakens each time a stranger approaches the door of the small apartment. Maria feels an immediate surge of danger, as if the stranger carries the same cruel intent that once shook her. The memory’s vividness heightens her vigilance; she now expects to be assaulted by any unfamiliar face. Even in the familiar corridor of her office—where she is a physical therapist helping patients with mobility—she senses threat when a new client steps in. The presence of strangers, once a normal part of her environment, now threatens her sense of safety, and the memory of abuse amplifies that threat. The threat that looms in her professional and personal spaces pushes Maria into a web of avoidance. At the clinic, she resists working with patients whose bodies or eyes remind her of the stranger she once feared, and she begins to keep the back of her chair against the wall, a small barrier that grants her a sense of containment. Outside of work, she spends hours cleaning her living room, the repetitive motions of her broom and mop offering a brief reprieve from the anxiety that gnaws at her. Each act of avoidance, she tells herself, prevents the threat from becoming real; the more she cleans, the less she feels exposed to the danger that lurks in every corner. Threat, however, does not remain a passive backdrop; it actively sparks the return of those memories. A sudden flash of a slammed door or the hiss of a stranger’s voice can bring a fragment of the abuse to the surface, dislodged from its dormant state by the tension of perceived danger. These sudden pieces of memory appear without warning, intruding into her thoughts as if a child’s toy were thrown into a well‑lit room. The intrusions are sharp, brief, and then vanish, leaving Maria rattled and more determined to fortify her surroundings against the threat that has awakened them. In the same way, Maria’s compulsive cleaning can backfire, feeding the memory cycle. While she believes she is keeping her environment safe, the act of rearranging items—sliding a towel from one shelf to another—can stir up the forgotten details of the abuse. She notices that the more she insists on order, the more her mind conjures images of the boy’s fists and the coldness of the apartment’s corners. The act of cleaning becomes a double‑edged sword, both a shield against threat and a trigger that pulls memories back into the foreground. Now, at 59, Maria has stopped attending her own appointments and instead seeks help because her avoidance has begun to interfere with her work and her relationships. She fears that if she does not confront the cycle, the fear of strangers and the compulsion to clean will consume her entire life, leaving her unable to provide care to others or maintain any semblance of normalcy. She hopes to regain control—not over the memories themselves, but over how they influence her daily life—so she can resume the meaningful work that once gave her a sense of purpose.
